01.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalls his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert who studied with Rabbi Akiva. Minyamin said that he, a first-generation Egyptian convert, had married another first-generation Egyptian convert, and that he planned to marry off his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so that his grandson would be allowed to enter the congregation. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yohanan told the teacher reciting this account to change it: Minyamin meant to marry his son to a first-generation convert.
01.why: The Gemara is asking whether a child's generation is counted from the father or the mother. Rava uses Minyamin's plan to challenge the view, credited to Rabbi Yohanan, that the father decides; the corrected wording answers him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports what his friend Minyamin told him.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: An Egyptian convert, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda and a student of Rabbi Akiva, planning whom his son should marry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who cites this account as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who told the reciter to correct the wording of the account.

terms.meaning: The Torah says Egyptians who join the Jewish people may marry into the community only from the third generation. A first- or second-generation Egyptian convert may not marry a born Jew.
To be allowed to marry a born Jew.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
Here, a person whose job was to memorize and recite early teachings word for word.

02.note: A man living in Rabbi Ami's neighborhood was publicly declared by Rabbi Ami to be a mamzer. The man went about weeping. Rabbi Ami told him: I have given you life.
02.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Yehuda that a mamzer who is publicly known survives, while one who is not known dies at the hand of Heaven. Rabbi Ami's words to the weeping man apply that teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who declared his neighbor a mamzer and then told him he had been given life.

terms.meaning: A child born of a forbidden union, such as adultery or incest. A mamzer may not marry a born Jew, and the status passes to his descendants.

03.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls going to learn Torah from Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The students there ganged up on him like the fighting roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study. He managed to learn only one thing: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a man who has intercourse with a hermaphrodite is liable to stoning, as if with a male.
03.why: The mishna quotes Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite, and the Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Eliezer does not treat a hermaphrodite as a full male. This memory of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms the wording of that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: A Sage, called simply Rabbi, who tells of his attempt to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua
people.about: The teacher whose students would not let Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learn.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose ruling on a hermaphrodite was the one thing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learned there.

terms.meaning: A person with both male and female sexual organs, whose legal status the Sages debate.
The severest form of court execution in Jewish law, prescribed for certain forbidden sexual acts, including relations between males.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

04.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, a priest, used to collect first tithe from a certain garden. Rabbi Akiva went and moved the garden's entrance so that it faced the cemetery, where a priest may not go. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said: Akiva comes with his satchel, and I have to live?
04.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds the first tithe belongs only to Levites, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that a priest may receive it too. This episode shows each acting on his view; afterwards the Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva blocked the entrance.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A priest who held that priests may receive the first tithe, and collected it from this garden.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who held the first tithe goes only to Levites, and moved the garden's entrance.

terms.meaning: A tenth of produce that the Torah gives to the Levites, the tribe that served in the Temple.
A descendant of Aaron. Priests may not become impure through contact with the dead, so they may not enter a cemetery.

05.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says he heard that a court may flog and punish beyond what the Torah requires, not to break the Torah but to build a fence around it. His example: in the days of the Greeks, a man rode a horse on Shabbat. He was brought to court and stoned, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
05.why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages have the power to uproot a Torah law. This report of a court executing a man for an act the Torah does not punish by death is brought as evidence that they can.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who reports what he heard about a court's power to punish, with this incident as his example.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. Riding a horse on Shabbat is forbidden by rabbinic law, not by the Torah itself.
Executed by stoning, the severest form of court execution, which the Torah sets for serious Shabbat violations.
The period of Greek rule over the Land of Israel.

06.note: A man had relations with his own wife under a fig tree, in public view. He was brought to court and flogged, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
06.why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages can uproot a Torah law by an active deed. This second precedent, after the man stoned for riding on Shabbat, seems to say they can; the Gemara limits it to safeguarding the Torah.

terms.meaning: Given lashes, a punishment a court could impose.

07.note: Rabbi Yannai's sharecropper used to bring him a basket of fruit every Friday. One Friday he was late, so Rabbi Yannai set aside tithe from fruit in his house on behalf of the fruit not yet delivered, and then asked Rabbi Hiyya whether this worked. Rabbi Hiyya told him he had acted well, citing a verse about tithing on Shabbat. Rabbi Yannai said he had dreamed the words "bruised reed" and feared it meant he had leaned on something weak. Rabbi Hiyya answered that the dream meant a different verse: "A bruised reed he shall not break."
07.why: The Gemara is listing Sages who hold that a person can act on something that does not yet exist or is not yet his. This episode is its proof that Rabbi Yannai, like Rabbi Hiyya, holds that view.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage who owned land worked by a sharecropper and tithed fruit that had not yet arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Yannai consulted, who approved what he had done and read his dream.

terms.meaning: A tenant farmer who works someone else's land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
A portion of produce that must be set aside before it may be eaten. It may not be set aside on Shabbat.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

08.note: A man had relations with his mother-in-law. Rav Yehuda had him brought and flogged. Rav Yehuda told him: If Shmuel had not said that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, I would make your wife forbidden to you for ever.
08.why: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a man who sleeps with his mother-in-law becomes forbidden to his wife, and Shmuel ruled against him. This case shows Rav Yehuda following Shmuel's ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who judged the man and reported Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who ruled that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An earlier Sage who held that such a man is forbidden to his wife.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

09.note: Rabbi Elazar taught a ruling in the study hall without saying he had it from his teacher Rabbi Yohanan, and Rabbi Yohanan was angry. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to calm him by recalling how Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei once argued so fiercely in the synagogue of Tiberias that a Torah scroll was torn, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma predicted that the synagogue would become a place of idol worship, as it did. That made Rabbi Yohanan angrier: were they now making his student his colleague? Then Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi pointed out that Joshua taught without saying "Moses told me," yet everyone knew it was Moses' Torah; so too everyone knows Rabbi Elazar's teaching is Rabbi Yohanan's. Rabbi Yohanan was calmed.
09.why: The ruling Rabbi Elazar repeated is the one just discussed, about a minor's relations with his yevama. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Yohanan's anger: a Sage quoted by name in this world, his lips move in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The teacher who was angered that his ruling was taught without his name.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's student, who taught the ruling without naming him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sages who tried to calm Rabbi Yohanan and made him angrier.

people.name: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage who succeeded in calming Rabbi Yohanan; Rabbi Yohanan later praised him.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma
people.about: A Sage present at the argument in Tiberias who predicted the synagogue's fate.

terms.meaning: The house of learning where the Sages taught and debated.
The handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, treated with great reverence.
Jewish law; here, a specific legal ruling.

10.note: Rabbi Yosei reports a case: Niftayim, a convert, married the wife of his brother from the same mother. The case came before the Sages, who said that a convert has no marriage. The Gemara objects that a convert's marriage is surely valid, and rereads the ruling to mean that the ban on a brother's wife does not apply to a convert.
10.why: Rav Aha bar Yaakov and Rav Sheshet disagree over a convert and his maternal brother's wife. This case is offered as proof that it is permitted even if the brother married her after converting; the Gemara answers that he married her before.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the case.

people.name: Niftayim
people.about: A convert who married the wife of his brother from the same mother.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
The Torah forbids a man to marry his brother's wife, apart from the special case of levirate marriage.

11.note: Ben Yasiyan traveled to cities overseas and found a convert married to the wife of his brother from the same mother. He asked: My son, who allowed you this? The convert pointed to a woman and her seven sons and said that on this very bench Rabbi Akiva sat and taught two things: a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife, and God spoke to Jonah only twice, not a third time.
11.why: The Gemara is asking whether a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife even when the brother married her after converting. This account is offered as proof; the Gemara answers that the brother married her before converting, then asks whether the convert can be trusted.

people.name: Ben Yasiyan
people.about: A Sage who met the convert on his travels and questioned him.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who, according to the convert, permitted this marriage.

people.name: Jonah
people.about: The biblical prophet, mentioned in the second teaching of Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
God's presence as it reveals itself to people, here in speaking to a prophet.
Coastal cities beyond the Land of Israel.

12.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said that in all his life he testified only once, and on his word a slave was promoted to the status of a priest. The Gemara objects that God would not let the righteous cause such a mistake, so he must mean that they almost promoted the slave. It explains how: he had seen the man receive teruma in Rabbi Yosei's town, then testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's town, where receiving teruma was taken as proof that a man is a priest.
12.why: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei disagree on whether teruma may be handed to a priest's slave without his master, because in Rabbi Yehuda's town receiving teruma was taken as proof of priestly lineage. This account shows what that local difference could lead to.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: A Sage whose one testimony nearly led to a slave being treated as a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage in whose town teruma was handed to a priest's slave, without this proving lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage in whose town receiving teruma was treated as proof of being a priest.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households may eat.
Granted the presumed status of a priest, with its privileges and restrictions, on the strength of evidence such as testimony.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

13.note: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house, and Rav Kahana asked him to come up and make a fifth judge for a halitza. Rav Kahana recalled that Rav Yehuda once told him to go up to the bundle of reeds and join the five. When people asked Rav Yehuda why five were needed, he said it was to make the matter public.
13.why: The Gemara has ruled that halitza needs only three judges, and that it takes place at a set location. These cases of five judges at a fixed spot explain why the Sages sometimes used more: to publicize it, not because the law requires it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Kahana, who was asked to make up the five.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who invited Rav Ashi to join and recalled an earlier case with Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher, who used five judges for halitza to make it public.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A spot marked by a bundle of reeds, set aside as the regular place where the court met for halitza.

14.note: Rav Yehuda asked Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to go up to the bundle of reeds and make a fifth judge for a halitza, to make the matter public. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda answered that a halitza court must be made of born Israelites, not converts, and he was a convert. Rav Yehuda said he would take money from someone on the word of a man like Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda. The Gemara objects that the Torah needs two witnesses, and explains that he meant he would cancel a loan document on his word.
14.why: The discussion is about who may sit on a court for halitza. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's refusal leads the Gemara to Rava's rule on when a convert may judge, and to why a halitza judge needs two Jewish-born parents.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who asked his student to join the halitza court and then praised his honesty.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A convert who declined to sit on the halitza court because he was a convert.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A spot marked by a bundle of reeds, set aside as the regular place where the court met for halitza.
A person who has joined the Jewish people rather than being born into it.
A written loan document that lets the lender collect the debt.

15.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of a trip to the city of Netzivin, where he met an Elder who knew Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira well; the Sage often ate at his table. Asked whether he had seen Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira conduct halitza, the Elder said many times. Asked whether with a soft shoe or a sandal, he replied: Does anyone perform halitza with a soft shoe? Rabbi Yosei asked him why, then, Rabbi Meir said halitza with a soft shoe is valid. Rabbi Yaakov reports in Rabbi Meir's name that it is allowed from the start.
15.why: The Gemara has been asking whether halitza may be done with a soft leather shoe from the start, or is only valid after the fact. It cites this account to show that early Sages disagreed on it, then asks the reason of those who forbid it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who traveled to Netzivin and questioned an Elder there.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage of Netzivin who often ate at the Elder's table and conducted halitza with a sandal.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who ruled that halitza with a soft shoe is valid.

people.name: Rabbi Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabbi Meir's view that a soft shoe may be used from the start.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
From the start; doing something as the preferred way, rather than accepting it only after it has been done.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

16.note: Abaye was with his teacher Rav Yosef when a widow came to perform halitza. Rav Yosef told Abaye to give the brother his sandal, and Abaye gave him his left one. Rav Yosef objected that the Sages allowed a left shoe only after the fact. Abaye answered that the same goes for a shoe that is not the brother's own. Rav Yosef explained that he had meant: give him the sandal and transfer ownership of it to him.
16.why: The mishna says halitza is valid with a shoe that is not the brother's own, and the Sages read "his shoe" as one that fits him. This episode shows that using a borrowed or left shoe is still not the ideal way.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who lent his left sandal for the halitza.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who was overseeing the halitza.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
Accepted as valid once done, though it should not be done that way to begin with (ab initio).

17.note: A widow came before Rabbi Ami for halitza, with Rabbi Abba bar Memel sitting before him, and she spat before removing the shoe. Rabbi Ami said: let her remove the shoe and the case is done. Rabbi Abba objected that she must spit, and asked why she should not simply spit again. Rabbi Ami said that would be a disaster: people would think the first spitting meant nothing and come to let a released widow marry the brothers. When Rabbi Abba objected that the steps must be in order, Rabbi Ami said the order is not essential. Rabbi Abba thought he was just being brushed off, but he went out, checked, and found a teaching that either order is valid.
17.why: The Gemara is weighing a ruling sent to Shmuel's father: a widow who spat first need only remove the shoe and need not spit again. This case is cited as an instance of that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage overseeing the halitza, who ruled that she did not need to spit again.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Memel
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rabbi Ami who challenged his ruling, then confirmed it.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
A widow who has already gone through halitza; she may no longer marry any of the brothers.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

18.note: Levi went out to the villages, and people asked him three questions: may a woman without arms perform halitza; is it valid if a widow spat blood; and does the verse about "the writing of truth" imply there is writing in Heaven that is not true? He had no answer, so he went and asked in the study hall. There he was told that the Torah does not say she must remove the shoe by hand, nor that she must spit saliva. On the verse, the answer was that a decree sealed with an oath can never be canceled, while one without an oath can.
18.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Abba bar Memel checked a halitza ruling in the study hall. Levi's questions bring more halitza cases, and his third question leads into the discussion of a decree sealed with an oath, shown by the house of Eli.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who went to teach in the villages and brought their questions back to the study hall.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
The house of learning where the Sages taught and debated.

19.note: Rabba taught that a descendant of the house of Eli cannot gain atonement through sacrifice, but can through Torah study. Abaye taught that he can through acts of kindness. Both were themselves from the house of Eli: Rabba, who devoted himself to Torah, lived forty years, and Abaye, who devoted himself to Torah and kindness, lived sixty.
19.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just shown from the oath against Eli's house that a sentence sealed with an oath cannot be torn up, even with offerings. Rabba and Abaye read that verse as leaving another way out.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and lived forty years.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and kindness and lived sixty years.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the Book of Samuel. God swore that their sin would not be atoned for by sacrifice, and that they would die young.
Good deeds done for others, such as helping the needy, visiting the sick and burying the dead.
Animal and grain offerings brought at the Temple, among other things to atone for sin.

20.note: A family in Jerusalem had members who kept dying at around eighteen years old. They came and told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said: perhaps you are from the family of Eli, of whom it is written that all their offspring shall die as young men; go and study Torah, and you will live. They went and studied Torah and lived, and people called them the family of Yohanan, after him.
20.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabba and Abaye, descendants of Eli, lived longer through Torah and kindness. This account from the Sages is a second example that Torah study can overcome the decree against Eli's house.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage the family turned to, who told them to study Torah.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the Book of Samuel. God swore that their sin would not be atoned for by sacrifice, and that they would die young.
